title: Building a KPI cadence that 10+ regions actually follow
excerpt: A KPI framework only matters if every region reviews the same numbers on the same rhythm. Notes on making that stick.
body:
When execution is spread across more than ten operating regions, the biggest risk is rarely a bad plan. It is that each region measures progress differently, so leadership discovers problems late.

Start with fewer numbers

A cadence works when the list of metrics is short enough to be read aloud in a meeting. Pick the handful of indicators that genuinely tell you whether a region is on track, and define each one so precisely that two people cannot compute it two ways.

Make the rhythm non-negotiable

The same review, at the same time, with the same template. Consistency turns a dashboard into a habit, and habits are what change behaviour on the ground.

Visibility is not reporting. Visibility is being able to act before the month closes.

Close the loop

Every review should end with owners and dates. Numbers without actions are just a scoreboard.

title: What an ERP rollout teaches you about reporting accuracy
excerpt: Rolling a system out to 120+ field and HQ users forces every hidden process assumption into the open.
body:
An ERP implementation is often described as a technology project. In practice it is a process-design project that happens to need software.

The system exposes the process

Before go-live, gaps in approvals, ownership and data entry are absorbed by people working around them. Once the system enforces a workflow, every workaround becomes visible.

Train for the field, not the head office

Reporting accuracy depends on the person entering the data, not the person reading the report. Field users need short, role-specific guidance more than a full system tour.

Measure adoption, not just delivery

A rollout is finished when reports are trusted, not when the last user has a login.

title: From finance business partner to CFO: widening the lens
excerpt: What changes when your remit grows from supporting initiatives to owning capital, controls and the board conversation.
body:
A business partner role teaches you to translate strategy into numbers for one team at a time. A CFO role asks you to hold the whole picture and decide where capital should not go.

Depth becomes judgement

Modelling skills stay essential, but the value shifts to deciding which questions deserve a model at all.

The board conversation

Investors and directors want clarity on risk, runway and return. Simple, consistent reporting earns more trust than impressive complexity.

Stay close to operations

The best finance leaders never lose contact with the teams generating the numbers.

title: Blended capital for MSMEs: pairing micro-equity with loan financing
excerpt: Why a mix of micro-equity and debt can unlock growth for small businesses that neither instrument serves well on its own.
body:
Small and medium enterprises often sit in an awkward gap. They are too small for institutional equity and too thinly documented for comfortable bank lending. A blended structure can bridge that gap.

Why blend?

Micro-equity gives a business patient capital and shares risk with the investor. Loan financing brings discipline and a defined repayment path. Together they can reduce the cost of capital and the strain on cash flow.

Designing the structure

The split should follow the use of funds: long-lived assets and growth investments suit equity-like risk, while working capital and predictable purchases suit debt. Repayment terms should be sized to realistic cash generation, not to optimistic forecasts.

Deploying in stages

Releasing capital against milestones protects both sides and creates natural checkpoints for review.

The goal is not to raise the most capital. It is to raise the right capital, in the right shape, at the right time.

title: Reading an early-stage startup like an analyst: market, viability, trajectory
excerpt: A practical structure for assessing market potential, financial viability and growth trajectory before you commit capital.
body:
Early-stage due diligence is less about precise forecasts and more about testing whether the story hangs together.

Market potential

Look for a customer problem that is real, frequent and paid for today. Size the market from the bottom up, starting with how many customers you can genuinely reach.

Financial viability

Unit economics come first. If each customer does not eventually pay back the cost of winning and serving them, growth only accelerates the loss.

Growth trajectory

Ask what has to be true for the next stage of growth and whether the team has evidence for each assumption.

Decide, then document

Write the investment case and its risks in plain language. It becomes the reference point for every later review.

title: Getting through CFA Level III as a working finance leader
excerpt: Reflections on balancing an executive workload with the final level of the CFA programme.
body:
Passing CFA Level III in August 2025 while holding a senior operating role taught me as much about time and priorities as it did about portfolio management.

Protect the routine

Consistent, shorter sessions beat occasional marathons. Fixing study blocks in the calendar, and treating them like board meetings, made the difference.

Connect study to work

Concepts around risk, allocation and client objectives map directly onto capital allocation decisions in a growing company. Applying them in real decisions makes them stick.

Keep the bigger goal in view

The charter is a credential, but the lasting value is a disciplined way of thinking about risk and return.
